examples: This system has been widely accepted not only in urban areas but also in rural regions.
He speaks not only English but also Chinese fluently.
Environmental problems matter not only to a single country but also to the international community.
This medicine not only suppresses the symptoms but is also effective in treating the cause.
Online education is in demand not only among students but also among working adults.
fields.explain:
Used in reports, academic writing, press releases, and formal speeches.
Part B should match A in word class/aspect (parallelism); avoid combining A and B of very different types unless it is a deliberate rhetorical choice.
「も」 usually attaches to the noun/particle of B: でも/にも/も.
Can be used with scope: A（範囲）＋のみならず、B（範囲）＋も to widen it.

～のみならず～も expresses “not only A but also B”, with a formal, written-language nuance. B usually widens the scope compared with A, or adds an equally important aspect. The form A＋のみならず、B＋も/まで/さえ… is common.
• Formal listing: emphasizes that A is only one example, and B (and possibly more) is also true.
• 「も」 is placed in the second clause to emphasize B; sometimes 「まで」「さえ」 are used instead of 「も」 to heighten the surprise.
• Close in meaning to ～だけでなく・～ばかりか, but 「のみならず」 is formal and has the nuance of argumentative writing.
fields.notes:
• In very formal writing, you may see「A のみならず、B に至るまで」 to emphasize an extremely wide scope.
• If B is very surprising, you can use「も」→「まで/さえ」: 彼は英語のみならず、中国語さえ独学した。
• Keep grammatical parallelism between A and B so the sentence is coherent: N with N, V with V (nominalized form when needed).
mistakes: Forgetting 「も」 in the second clause: use B＋も/にも/でも to follow the pattern correctly.
Using it in casual speech sounds stiff; in everyday conversation, 「だけでなく」 is used.
Mixing non-parallel word classes between A and B makes the sentence unnatural.
Joining a very long A without a comma after 「のみならず」 makes it hard to read; add a break.

rows: Not only A but also B
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>だけでなく<ruby>中国語<rt>ちゅうごくご</rt></ruby>も
Not only A, but B as well
Emphatic, often with a stronger nuance of surprise than 「のみならず」
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったばかりか<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>も
A goes without saying, and B too
Assumes A is obvious; lighter nuance
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>はもちろん<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>も
Similar in terms of scope; less formal
<ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らず<ruby>高齢<rt>こうれい</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>も

examples: I'm happy to be able to do research under a famous professor.
I was raised by my parents with plenty of love.
This project is being carried out under the direction of the mayor.
In Japan, everyone is equal under the law.
I'm grateful to be able to live in peace.
fields.explain:
の下で is mostly used for specific people or direct guidance: “under the teaching of…”, “under the leadership of…”.
のもとで is used for abstract, broad things such as laws, policies, and conditions: “under the law”, “under peaceful skies…”.
Style: Formal, common in written language, speeches, and newspapers, JLPT N2~N1.
Not used in casual conversation when simply saying “under a tree” → in that case use ～の下に (物理).

•
Expresses the environment, conditions, or influence under which an action/event takes place.

•
Means “under”, “under the management/influence of…” – often used with nouns referring to people, organizations, the law, or protection.

•
の下で (のもとで): Emphasizes the direct direction, guidance, or influence of a person (teacher, doctor, coach…).

•
のもとで (のもとで): More formal; emphasizes scope, conditions, or principles (the law, peace, government…).
fields.notes:
• Remember: の下で＝direct influence, のもとで＝broad environment/rules.
• In legal contexts it expresses “everyone is equal under…”, so it appears often on the JLPT.
• In everyday conversation with the physical meaning “under a tree, under a table”, this pattern is not used.
meaning_vi: Under the (direction/guidance/influence) of…
examples: 1. ①　〈感謝を述べる〉先生のもとで勉強できて、本当によかったです。
2. ②　人の性格は、どういう親のもとで育ってかで、全く異なってくる。
meaning_vi: 条件(じょうけん)、指導(しどう)、支配(しはい)等(など)の下(もと)で
Under (management, direction, etc.)
examples: 1. 晴れた空のもとで運動会が盛大に行われた。
Under clear skies, the sports day was held on a grand scale.
2. 女の子は両親の温かい愛情のもとですっくすくと育った。
The girl grew up quickly in the warm love of her parents.
3. 選挙は国連の管理のもとで行われた。
The election was held under the supervision of the United Nations.
4. 「ぜひ鈴木先生の下で研究させていただきたいと思っております」
I would very much like to do research under the guidance of Professor Suzuki.
5. ～を表面上の理由にして（-）の行為が行われている
6. 開発の名のもとに自然破壊が進み、さまざまな問題が生じている。
In the name of development, the destruction of nature is advancing, causing many problems.
7. 一部の学校では、教育の名のもとに体罰が行われているそうだ。
It is reported that in some schools, corporal punishment is carried out in the name of education.
explain: A formal expression typical of written language.
examples: 1. 子どもたちが青空の下で元気に遊んでいる。
The children are playing energetically under the blue sky.
2. 田中先生のご指導の下、研究論文を書いています。
I am writing a research paper under the guidance of Professor Tanaka.
mistakes: Confusing it with the physical meaning (under a table, under a tree…) → this pattern is not used for that.
Using it in ordinary spoken language sounds unnatural; use it in written language, newspapers, and essays.
Dropping の after the preceding noun → grammatically incorrect (の is required).

rows: Direct influence from an individual or organization.
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>で<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>ぶ。
<ruby>法律<rt>ほうりつ</rt></ruby>のもとで<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>られている。
Emphasizes following rules/a process of change.
<ruby>指示<rt>しじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>従<rt>したが</rt></ruby>って<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>く。
Based on…, in the name of…
Close to のもとで but means “on the grounds of”.
<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>のもとに<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>した。

fields.meaning:
～か（どうか）わからない
No idea whether
fields.connection: V/Aい plain form + のやら/ものやら / N・Naな + のやら/ものやら
examples: Lee has no expression on his face, so I can't tell whether he understands the class or not.
These days there are young people dressed so that you can't tell whether they're men or women.
There's a dry-cleaning tag on his coat. Should I tell him, or would it be better not to?
The kids haven't come home. Where on earth are they, and what are they doing?
"Huh, my glasses are gone. Where did I put them?"
* ・Who knows when that was ・What on earth is that about

fields.meaning:
～かどうかは…しだいだ
Depends on, rests on
examples: Whether I pass or not depends on how hard I work over the next month.
Whether the contract succeeds depends on how our business partner views these conditions.
"Whether I can be happy depends on your answer."
Whether we can achieve our goal depends on how thoroughly we've prepared in advance.
* "Whether this project succeeds or not rests on your shoulders."
It may not look great, but the taste is excellent.
Never mind the cost; please keep to the deadline.
Whatever the result, taking on the challenge is meaningful.
My Japanese aside, I can speak English without any problems.
Whether it's safe or not, it's certainly getting attention.
fields.explain:
N₂, which comes after, is usually the point the speaker wants to affirm/evaluate.
Soft, polite nuance; it does not deny the value of N₁.
Often used in discussions, negotiations, and evaluations of products/services.

• Setting A aside to discuss B: The speaker intentionally skips/does not consider A for now and shifts the focus to B.
• Soft contrast: Does not completely negate A; only gives priority to B in the context.
• Scope: Most common with nouns; with a clause, you must nominalize it with の/こと/かどうか.
fields.notes:
• Easily paired with noun pairs: 見た目／中身、価格／品質、量／質、形式／内容、結果／過程.
• When N₁ is long, use “～という点はともかく” to keep the sentence compact.
• In presentations, “前置きはともかく、本題は…” is very natural.
mistakes: Forgetting the particle “は” after N₂: it must be “N₁はともかく N₂は…”.
Using it with a bare adjective/verb: you need to nominalize it (～の/こと/かどうか).
Confusing it with “どころか”: exam traps test the degree of contrast. “はともかく” is not a strong negation.

rows: <ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>はさておき、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る。
Stronger sense of exclusion than “はともかく”.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby>として<ruby>真面目<rt>まじめ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いどころか<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>外見<rt>がいけん</rt></ruby>はともかくとして…

examples: Jokes are one thing, but hurtful remarks are unacceptable.
Standing is still OK, but walking for a long time is impossible.
A beginner might, but a professional shouldn't make a mistake like that.
Contacting people in writing is fine, but I'm not good on the phone.
Rain is one thing, but snow has a major impact on traffic.
fields.explain:
The second clause is mostly negative/expresses difficulty, to highlight the limit of what is acceptable.
A mild nuance of criticism; it sets a social/personal standard.
In debates, it is used to reduce conflict: acknowledge part of it (A) and then reject (B).

• “A is still acceptable, but B is not”: Sets a minimum acceptable level (A). B goes beyond that threshold, so it is rejected/hard to accept.
• Evaluation nuance: Usually followed by a negative/difficulty in the second clause (～ない／無理だ／困る／許せない).
• Scope of use: Natural with nouns; with a verb/adjective, nominalize it with の.
fields.notes:
• Common noun pairs: 冗談／嘘、雨／雪、初心者／プロ、遅刻／無断欠勤、立つ／走る、挨拶／説教.
• With verbs, a symmetrical structure with のは…のは… keeps the sentence coherent: V₁のはまだしも、V₂のは…
• Avoid it when A and B are not on the same level of criteria (hard to compare).
mistakes: Dropping the particle “は” after part B: it must be “Aはまだしも、Bは…”.
The second clause is not negative/unpleasant: this weakens the meaning. Use 無理だ／問題だ／ダメだ…
Confusing it with “はともかく”: an exam trap contrasting shifting the focus vs. setting a level of acceptance.

rows: If it were A, it would still be OK
Emphasizes supposition/condition; about as common as “はまだしも”.
Shifts the focus; does not compare levels of acceptance.
<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>はともかく<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>は…
Stronger, harsh negation; “まだしも” only indicates a minimum level of tolerance.
<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
General concessive supposition; “まだしも” leans toward comparing degree.
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしても<ruby>言<rt>いいすぎ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>過<rt></rt></ruby>ぎだ。

examples: Joking aside, let's talk seriously.
Let's leave work talk out of it today and just enjoy ourselves.
No flattery, it's really delicious.
I have an allergy, so do you have a menu without nuts?
You can't talk about this town's development without mentioning him.
fields.explain:
“N は抜きにして” steers the topic: used when you want to ask someone to focus/change the topic.
“N抜きで/抜きに/抜きの” describes the state of “without A” (food, services…).
In formal contexts, it can be replaced with “～はさておき／～はともかく”.
Avoid using it as a blunt command to a superior; add a polite softener:失礼ですが、冗談は抜きにして…

• “Setting aside…, leaving out…, no talk of…”: removes an element A from the conversation/situation to focus on the main point.
• With things/ingredients: means “without A/with no A added”.
• Often used to change direction in a conversation or meeting: cut off joking/beating around the bush to get to the point.
• Direct, sometimes strong nuance; consider politeness depending on the listener.
fields.notes:
• “お世辞抜きで/冗談抜きで” are set phrases, shortened without は.
• With food: “～抜きでお願いします” is very natural when ordering (氷抜きで/ネギ抜きで…).
• “N を抜きにしては” is a different pattern: a necessary condition; do not confuse it with “N は抜きにして”. meaning_vi: Leave… out, stop… ⏐ explain: Used to say that something is no longer to be done.
It means ｢…は除いて｣(remove that),「は止めて」(stop that) ⏐ examples: 1. 皆さん、仕事の話は抜きにして楽しく飲みましょう。
Everyone, let's drop the work talk and enjoy our drinks together.
2. お世辞抜きに、君の日本語は本当にうまいよ。
I'm not just flattering you, your Japanese is really good.
3. 田中さん抜きで（は）パーティーは始められません。
We can't start the party without Mr. Tanaka.
mistakes: Confusing it with “～なしで”: the JLPT tests the difference in nuance between changing the topic (抜きにして) and the state of not having something (なしで).
Using “は抜きにして” about sensitive matters (someone else's contribution) can sound rude; mind your politeness.
Wrong position of は: × 抜きには冗談して → ○ 冗談は抜きにして

rows: Leave A aside to discuss B
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>抜<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>きにして…
<ruby>詳細<rt>しょうさい</rt></ruby>はさておき、<ruby>結論<rt>けつろん</rt></ruby>を。
Neutral, less of a “cutting off” nuance
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>た<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>はともかく、<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>い。
Common vocabulary, no implication of changing the topic

fields.meaning: It's not as if just… is enough
examples: Being cheap isn't everything. Quality matters too.
Being fast isn't enough. Safety comes first.
Explaining something doesn't necessarily make people understand. You only really understand through experience.
Having a good education doesn't guarantee success.
Practicing a lot doesn't automatically make you improve. Quality matters too.
fields.explain:
Placed after a conditional clause “～ば/～であれば/～なら”. What comes before is usually a single criterion.
A rebutting tone, gentle but instructive/normative.
Often followed by a contrasting element in the second clause to state the right criterion: ～も必要だ／～こそ重要だ。

• “It's not as if just… means…”: Rebuts an oversimplified view (cheap, fast, a lot… is good).
• Pragmatics: Used in argumentation, explanation, and criticism. Often used with evaluative words such as いい／十分／大丈夫／完璧.
• Normative: Implies “condition A is only one part; other factors are needed”.
fields.notes:
• Easily combined with pairs of contrasting adjectives: 速い・安全、安い・品質、高い・価値、量・質.
• In written language, a nominalized structure often comes before this pattern: ～であるからといって… but keep “～というものでもない” to conclude the argument.
mistakes: Dropping the ば condition: “安いというものでもない” is not wrong but lacks the contrast; exam questions usually require “安ければ”.
Using it with obvious facts: “酸素がなければ生きられるというものでもない” is logically wrong.
Mixing it up with “とは限らない”: Both are general negations, but the JLPT requires the right nuance of “a norm/a single criterion”.

rows: ～からといって～とは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない
Just because A doesn't mean B
More conversational; negates a possibility in general, does not emphasize a norm.
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いからといって<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない。
Partial negation; does not need the ば condition.
Affirms a rule; the pattern being studied negates a “simple” rule.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>報<rt>むく</rt></ruby>われるものだ。

examples: Everyone was impressed by the way he works.
She speaks calmly and persuasively.
Today the sun came out for the first time in a week.
Meeting again after ten years, I couldn't hold back my tears.
Seeing the way he drank, I felt he must be very tired.
fields.explain:
N + ぶり emphasizes “the way/appearance” and implies an evaluation (can be praise or criticism).
Time + ぶり（に）: used to say “for the first time in…”; it can come before a noun (～ぶりのN) or serve as the predicate (～ぶりだ).
Vます + っぷり is the natural choice when attaching to a verb to say “the way of …”.
In formal writing, ～ぶり meaning “way/manner” suits reports/evaluations:仕事ぶりの改善,指導ぶり,経営ぶり.

• Means “way/manner/appearance” when attached to a noun referring to a behavior: 話しぶり（way of speaking）、働きぶり（way of working）. Often implies an evaluation.
• Expresses “a period of time that has passed” when attached to a time expression: 十年ぶりに（for the first time in 10 years）、三日ぶりの雨（the first rain in 3 days).
• With verbs, the more natural form is Vます + っぷり: 食べっぷり（way of eating）, 飲みっぷり（way of drinking）. The form ～ぶり after Vます exists but is limited and sounds old-fashioned/less natural.
• Nuance: descriptive and objective, but often accompanied by the speaker's impression/evaluation (good/bad).
fields.notes:
• “～ぶり” comes from 振り (to swing/wave), which shifted to mean “look, appearance, manner”.
• In newspaper headlines: ～ぶり often emphasizes a strong impression: 迫力の演技ぶり（a powerful performance）.
• Time + ぶり can combine with inexact amounts: 久しぶり（it's been a long time）, しばらくぶり（after a while）.
mistakes: Confusing Vます + ぶり with っぷり: with verbs, use っぷり to sound more natural.
Forgetting に when used as a time adverbial: 十年ぶり会った（incorrect）→ 十年ぶりに会った（correct）.
Thinking ～ぶり only has a time meaning: in fact it also means “way/appearance”.
Using ～ぶり too subjectively to judge people in a formal context can be impolite; use it neutrally: 仕事ぶりを評価する.

rows: Attaches to a behavior noun; more formal than っぷり
Talks about a gap in time
<ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby>ぶりに<ruby>帰国<rt>きこく</rt></ruby>した
<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>／<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>しよう

fields.meaning: Going so far as to…, even…
examples: He went so far as to borrow money to keep gambling.
She stayed up all night just to play this game.
To think someone would even lie to their parents to raise money!
I don't want to prolong my life if it means having surgery.
There's no need to cry when you apologize.
Do you want to win so badly that you'd go that far?
fields.explain:
Emphasizes the “excessive/far-reaching” degree of the means/action used to reach a goal.
Often accompanied by an attitude of criticism or surprise, or advice not to go that far.
Best used with content that is negative/difficult/involves sacrifice; if positive, it needs a suitable context so it does not sound sarcastic.

• Expresses an extreme degree: “going so far as to even do … in order to …”. Often implies a negative or excessive evaluation.
• Two forms with the same meaning: Nまでして (even resorting to N) and Vてまで (going so far as to do V).
• Often followed by an evaluation of “unnecessary/not worth it”: ～までして／～てまで…する必要はない／そこまでして…？
fields.notes:
• Nまでして emphasizes “extreme means” (borrowing money, lying…); Vてまで emphasizes “extreme actions” (staying up all night, surgery…).
• Often appears in critical questions: そこまでして～たいの？／Vてまで～たいの？
• When used with a positive goal, add a reason to avoid sounding critical: 家族のために徹夜してまで働いた。
mistakes: Confusing it with “までに” (deadline): × 明日までして提出 → ○ 明日までに提出.
Wrong connection: “Nまでして” goes with nouns; “Vてまで” goes with the te-form of verbs.
Using it in a purely positive context makes the sentence sound sarcastic; the JLPT often tests the negative nuance.
Redundant “してまでして”: use “して” only once: × 借金してまでして → ○ 借金までして.

rows: Going so far as to … in order to …
<ruby>借金<rt>しゃっきん</rt></ruby>までして<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。
Only indicates inclusion, without the sense of “going far to reach a goal”
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>名<rt>な</rt></ruby>さえ<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れた。
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>。
No need to go as far as
Negates necessity; no sense of “going far”
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>するまでもない。
